---
title: "Correctness-Aware NL-to-SQL for Object-Centric Event Logs"
subtitle: "A typed-IR and verifier pipeline for translating business questions into DuckDB SQL"
description: "A correctness-aware natural-language query pipeline over object-centric ERP event logs."
---

## Overview

Most text-to-SQL demos hide the hard part by putting every answer in one table.
This project works with a less forgiving shape: object-centric order-to-cash
event logs, where a business question is often answered by moving through the
right path between objects.

An order item can connect to a customer, a billing document, an accounting
receivable item, a delivery item, a material, or a payer. Those paths are not
interchangeable. SQL can run cleanly and still answer the wrong question.

The pipeline treats generated SQL as something to compile, not something to
trust directly. A translator proposes typed intent. Deterministic code then
checks schema references, relation paths, SQL policy, and result traces before
anything executes.

## Running It End To End

For a local run that does not require an API key:

```powershell
py -3.11 -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .
.\.venv\Scripts\python scripts\create_demo_ocel.py --overwrite
.\.venv\Scripts\python -m pytest tests/ -q
```

That checks the package, verifier, compiler, and synthetic-data path. To run the
API with a cloud translator, copy `.env.example` to `.env`, set one provider
key, and start the Flask wrapper:

```powershell
$env:NL2OCEL_BACKEND = "deepseek"
$env:DEEPSEEK_API_KEY = Read-Host "DeepSeek API key"
.\scripts\start_api.ps1
```

Then send a question:

```powershell
curl "http://localhost:8000/query/How%20many%20order%20items%20are%20linked%20to%20a%20customer%20that%20received%20a%20dunning%20notice%3F"
```

OpenAI and Anthropic are supported with `NL2OCEL_BACKEND=openai` or
`NL2OCEL_BACKEND=anthropic` and the matching provider environment variable.
Benchmark summaries are saved in `outputs/reports/`. Recomputing them requires
compatible OCEL parquet files under `data/processed/ocel/`.

## The Data Shape

The query target is an object-centric event log represented as three DuckDB
views.

| Table | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `events` | Event type, timestamp, object id, and object type. |
| `objects` | Business objects such as order items, customers, billing documents, and AR items. |
| `relations` | Object-to-object links such as `order_to_customer`, `order_to_billing`, and `billing_to_ar`. |

The relation table is what makes this more than a normal text-to-SQL exercise.
It turns the problem from "find the right columns" into "find the right object
path."

```text
order_item --order_to_customer--> customer --event--> dunning_raised
order_item --order_to_billing--> billing_doc --billing_to_ar--> ar_item
```

If the question asks about customers who received dunning notices, the first
path is relevant. If it asks about payment clearing, the second path is. The
verifier makes that choice explicit instead of leaving it buried inside a SQL
string.

## The Design Decision

The typed intermediate representation is the core boundary in the system. It is
small enough to validate, but expressive enough to carry query intent, filters,
joins, aggregations, and ordering.

```json
{
  "intent": "path_relation",
  "tables": ["objects", "relations", "events"],
  "select": [
    {
      "col": "object_id",
      "agg": "COUNT",
      "alias": "n_orders_with_dunning_customer",
      "distinct": true
    }
  ],
  "filters": [
    {"table": "objects", "col": "object_type", "op": "=", "val": "order_item"},
    {"table": "events", "col": "event_type", "op": "=", "val": "dunning_raised"}
  ],
  "joins": [
    {"relation_type": "order_to_customer"}
  ]
}
```

Once a plan is structured this way, ordinary code can inspect it before SQL
runs. Tables, columns, enum values, relation types, predicates, and
aggregations become checkable. The architecture keeps interpretation and
execution apart: the translator handles language, while the verifier, compiler,
SQL policy, and result hashing define the executable path.

![Architecture of the correctness-aware NL-to-SQL pipeline.](site-assets/pipeline-architecture.svg){.wide-figure}

## Verification Layers

The checks live in code and configuration, not just prompt wording. The
translator can propose a plan, but accepted SQL must be compiled from verified
IR.

| Layer | File | What it blocks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schema catalog | `configs/schema_catalog.json` | Hallucinated tables, columns, event types, and object types. |
| Relation whitelist | `configs/relation_whitelist.json` | Unsupported object-centric joins. |
| IR verifier | `src/nl2ocel/query_verifier.py` | Invalid intents, predicates, aggregations, and relation paths. |
| SQL compiler | `src/nl2ocel/ir_to_sql.py` | Unverified generated SQL reaching the database. |
| SQL policy | `configs/sql_policy.yaml` | Write operations, disallowed tables, and disallowed SQL forms. |
| Result hashing | `src/nl2ocel/result_hash.py` | Alias and row-order noise when comparing predicted and gold answers. |

The boundary is simple: flexible interpretation on one side, deterministic
execution rules on the other.

## A Query Trace

One benchmark question asks:

> How many order items are linked to a customer that received a dunning notice?

The accepted SQL counts order items only through the whitelisted
`order_to_customer` path, and only when the customer object has a
`dunning_raised` event.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT o.object_id) AS n_orders_with_dunning_customer
FROM objects o
WHERE o.object_type = 'order_item'
  AND EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM relations r
    JOIN events e ON e.object_id = r.to_object_id
    WHERE r.from_object_id = o.object_id
      AND r.relation_type = 'order_to_customer'
      AND e.event_type = 'dunning_raised'
  )
```

In the smoke test, that path runs against parquet-backed DuckDB views, returns
one result row, and matches the saved gold result hash.

## From Question To Evidence

One benchmark row should be traceable all the way through the system. The
question supplies the natural-language intent and expected result hash; the
schema catalog and retriever constrain the vocabulary; the translator produces a
typed plan; the verifier decides whether that plan is admissible; the compiler
emits DuckDB SQL; execution produces rows, latency, status, and a denotation
hash; the report files aggregate those traces across methods and splits.

![Trace from a benchmark question to typed IR, verification, SQL execution, result hashing, and saved evaluation artifacts.](site-assets/question-to-evidence.svg){.wide-figure}

| Stage | Where it lives | What to read there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Question and gold answer | `benchmark/nl2ocel_benchmark_v1.csv` | Natural-language question, split, query class, and expected denotation hash. |
| Schema context | `configs/schema_catalog.json`, `src/nl2ocel/schema_retriever.py` | The tables, columns, enum values, and relation vocabulary shown to the translator. |
| Typed plan | `src/nl2ocel/nl_to_ir.py` | The structured intent the model is allowed to propose. |
| Verification boundary | `src/nl2ocel/query_verifier.py`, `configs/relation_whitelist.json`, `configs/sql_policy.yaml` | The checks that decide whether a plan can become SQL. |
| SQL and evidence | `src/nl2ocel/ir_to_sql.py`, `src/nl2ocel/result_hash.py`, `outputs/reports/` | The compiled query, execution status, latency, result hash, and aggregate metrics. |

## Experimental Setup

The saved runs use a fixed evaluation protocol rather than open-ended chat
sampling. Zero-shot means no demonstration examples in the prompt. Greedy
decoding means `temperature = 0.0` for the model call. The main comparison uses
DeepSeek Chat for B1, B2, B3, and the constrained pipeline; the cross-model
check reruns the constrained pipeline with DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, and Claude
Sonnet while keeping the verifier, compiler, policy, evaluator, and development
split fixed.

::: {.protocol-grid}
::: {.protocol-card}
**Greedy Decoding**

All provider calls set `temperature = 0.0` through `src/nl2ocel/llm_client.py`,
so the comparison is not driven by sampling variation. The default cap is
`2048` tokens. B1 uses `200`; DIN-SQL uses `600` for stages 1-3 and `350` for
self-correction, with stage stop sequences.
:::

::: {.protocol-card}
**Splits**

`120` benchmark questions across nine query classes: `74` development questions
and `46` held-out test questions. The few-shot baseline excludes its
demonstration seed questions from scoring.
:::

::: {.protocol-card}
**Zero-Shot / Few-Shot / DIN-SQL**

B1 follows Rajkumar-style zero-shot Create Table + Select 3 prompting, with no
demonstration examples. B2 uses Nan-style similarity-diversity few-shot
selection. B3 implements the four-stage DIN-SQL flow. The constrained pipeline
translates to typed IR before SQL.
:::

::: {.protocol-card}
**Scoring**

`ExecRate` records whether SQL runs. `DenAcc` compares value-only result hashes
against the gold answer. `JoinHall` counts relation types outside the whitelist.
Confidence intervals use `10,000` bootstrap samples with seed `42`.
:::
:::

## Evaluation

The benchmark contains 120 natural-language questions across nine query
classes: simple counts, top-k grouping, temporal trends, object-relation paths,
delay analysis, anomaly filters, conformance checks, nested aggregation, and
window aggregation.

![Denotation accuracy compares whether the returned table matches the gold answer, not whether the SQL string looks similar.](site-assets/denacc-comparison.svg)

Denotation accuracy asks whether the returned table matches the gold answer,
not whether the SQL text looks familiar. On the development split, the
constrained pipeline reaches `64.9%` denotation accuracy versus `41.9%`,
`12.5%`, and `40.5%` for the three baselines. On the held-out test split it
reaches `50.0%`, ahead of the same baselines at `41.3%`, `20.0%`, and `45.7%`.

![Accuracy and latency trade-off across the compared methods.](site-assets/accuracy-latency.svg)

The latency chart matters because checks only help if the system remains usable.
The constrained pipeline adds verification and repair, but its average latency
stays close to the zero-shot baseline and far below the few-shot baseline.

| Split | Method | n | ExecRate | DenAcc | JoinHall | Avg latency |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Dev | B1 Zero-shot | 74 | 86.5% | 41.9% | 1.4% | 2.1s |
| Dev | B2 Few-shot | 72 | 100.0% | 12.5% | 0.0% | 43.9s |
| Dev | B3 DIN-SQL | 74 | 66.2% | 40.5% | 0.0% | 10.0s |
| Dev | Constrained pipeline | 74 | 86.5% | **64.9%** | 0.0% | 3.3s |
| Test | B1 Zero-shot | 46 | 93.5% | 41.3% | 0.0% | 2.2s |
| Test | B2 Few-shot | 45 | 100.0% | 20.0% | 0.0% | 40.1s |
| Test | B3 DIN-SQL | 46 | 73.9% | 45.7% | 0.0% | 10.3s |
| Test | Constrained pipeline | 46 | 78.3% | **50.0%** | 0.0% | 3.3s |

`ExecRate` measures whether the SQL runs. `DenAcc` measures whether the result
hash matches the gold answer. `JoinHall` counts relation types outside the
whitelist. B2 excludes demonstration-seed questions from scoring, which is why
its `n` is slightly smaller.

## Cross-Model Robustness

The baseline comparison asks whether the architecture improves over other
prompting strategies. The backbone check asks a different question: does the
same boundary still hold when the translator changes? The run keeps the
verifier, compiler, relation whitelist, SQL policy, evaluator, and development
split fixed; only the translation backend changes.

![Cross-model comparison for the constrained pipeline on the development split.](site-assets/backbone-comparison.svg)

DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, and Claude Sonnet do not land on identical accuracy, but
all three stay inside the same execution boundary: zero off-whitelist joins in
the saved run. The point is not that every model behaves the same. The point is
that the system does not have to trust a model's SQL style to control what can
run.

## Engineering Trade-Off

The ablation adds an important wrinkle. Removing the verifier raises
development-set DenAcc in this run, but it also removes the typed boundary that
makes accepted SQL inspectable. The full version keeps verifier and policy
checks even when a looser variant looks attractive on one split.

![Component ablation showing execution rate and denotation accuracy across constrained pipeline variants.](site-assets/ablation-tradeoff.svg)

The measured trade-off is part of the result. The chosen architecture favors
auditable execution over a single leaderboard number.

## Where It Worked

![Per-class profile for the constrained pipeline, including coverage and accuracy by query class.](site-assets/class-profile.svg)

The constrained pipeline is strongest on temporal trends, path-relation
questions, nested aggregations, and delay analysis. Those are the classes where
typed intent and explicit relation paths carry the most signal.

Anomaly and window-style questions remain harder. They need richer semantic
templates and better coverage for edge cases such as rolling windows, missing
downstream activity, and high-delay thresholds.

The result is not a universal NL-to-SQL engine. It is a tested design for a
narrower requirement: generated queries over object-centric process data should
be inspectable, rejectable, and measurable.

## Takeaways

Direct NL-to-SQL is convenient, but convenience is not the same as correctness.
For object-centric process data, the relation path is part of the answer. This
project makes that path explicit, compiles only verified plans, and evaluates
answers by denotation rather than surface SQL similarity.

The reusable pattern is the separation of roles: use a translator for
interpretation, but put a typed representation, verifier, compiler, and policy
layer between generated text and the database.
